# The west quay

## Morning

The harbour kept a grey skin until the first boat cut it. She stood at the end of the west quay with a notebook that would not stay dry, and she wrote the names of the boats she knew and a blank line for the ones she did not. A man in a yellow coat hauled a crate and did not look up. The crane turned once, stopped, and turned back, as if it had forgotten the lift.

When the rain thickened she did not go in. The office behind her had a lamp in the window and a chair that faced the wrong way, toward the filing cabinet instead of the water. She had turned the chair last winter and nobody had turned it back. That small refusal pleased her more than it should have. She counted the gaps between the horns of the boats, then the gaps between the horns and the church clock, and she wrote only the gaps.

## The ledger

By noon the ledger on the rail had four columns: boat, gap, colour of the water, and whether anyone had waved. Most rows had no wave. The water stayed the colour of zinc. A child ran the length of the quay and was collected at the steps by someone who did not scold. The crane finished its forgotten lift and set a crate down as if the delay had been the plan.

She closed the notebook when the page went soft. The numbers were already in her head, which was the only dry place left. On the walk back she passed the bus stop and did not count the buses. The gaps belonged to the water that day, and borrowing them for the street would have muddied both lists.

# The east shed

## What was left

The shed smelled of rope and cold tea. Someone had written the tide times on the door in pencil and then crossed out the afternoon. She copied the morning times and left the crossed-out hour alone. A coil of rope had been moved from the left wall to the right, and the dust showed the old circle. She noted the move and not the rope. Objects were only there to show that a place had changed.

The lamp from the office window was visible through a gap in the boards. It was still on. She wondered who would switch it off, and then she stopped wondering, because the question was a bus and not a gap. Outside, the rain eased into a fine mist that did not quite fall. The quay shone. She put the notebook in the inside pocket and buttoned the coat over it, and she walked the long way around the shed so she would not have to pass the crane again.
